title: Yowie on the Loose: the Spring of our Discontent
excerpt: While we look forward to the morning tea of blue cupcakes on International Men’s Day (Thursday 19 November), Wednesday’s Rugby News has the Kiwi Press pull apart the All Blacks’ deficiencies, some Rassie post-loss carry-on and a potential blood test for CTE. content:
While we look forward to the morning tea of blue cupcakes on International Men’s Day (Thursday 19 November), Wednesday’s Rugby News has the Kiwi Press pull apart the All Blacks’ deficiencies, some Rassie post-loss carry-on and a potential blood test for CTE.

NZ press comments read a lot like criticism of poor Wallaby games

PlanetRugby has summarised the best of the NZ media comments on New Zealand’s historic 35-28 loss to Wales at Pontypandy Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Saturday. Some comments remind this writer of criticism of the Wallabies over the years after their bad games:

“They dominated possession and territory in the second half in the same way Lada dominated the Soviet car market, and yet for all the time they had on the ball, they couldn’t find a way to score the points they needed.”

“In the last 10 minutes the All Blacks had 70 percent of possession and overall they had 63% territory. It counted for nothing when it mattered.“

“But like 2007, the All Blacks resorted to one-off runners coming in wave after wave and while Wales’ defence has to be credited for the security of its tackling and ability to reset, it was made a little easy for them by New Zealand’s ill-conceived tactical approach.”

“The All Blacks looked like a team struggling to make good decisions under pressure, and the fact they found themselves chasing the game in the final quarter is primarily because they again didn’t have enough innovation or accuracy.”

“There were high-risk offloads, acts of ill-discipline and a 10-minute black spot at the start of each half where they simply didn’t play.”

“Loose offloads, several of which went to Welshmen, were an unwanted feature of the All Blacks’ game,”

“Clearly they had a desire to operate at maximum revs, and wanted to back their athleticism and ball handling to get in behind the opposition defensive line, but the execution let them down too often.”

“Mistakes stalled momentum.”

Wit kant watch

Innovator and second coming of the Messiah, Rassie Erasmus, had plenty to say in the press after the Cheese-Eating Surrender Monkeys beat his Dutch Dirt Farmers 21:19 over the weekend.

The BBC (grow up!) reports that Erasmus has predicted Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast will not face a ban after being cited, and questioned what he perceived as double standards in officiating to the point where he asked: “is that not match-fixing?”

“I must say the right words now. We are in the northern hemisphere. I think there is going to be a technicality and he is going to play,” Erasmus said when asked about Prendergast being cited.

When he was asked to elaborate on what he meant by a “technicality”, Erasmus said that, while he is “not a legal guy”, “it never seems to go our way”.

“I’m not saying anybody’s doing anything wrong. I’m just not expecting him to get [suspended] – I think he’ll play on Saturday,” Erasmus said.

Erasmus, who said “I swear I’m not moaning”, also pointed to how Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong avoided punishment for an alleged groin grab in Leinster’s United Rugby Championship win over Munster in October.

Last year, South Africa prop Jan-Hendrik Wessels was handed a nine-match ban for a similar offence and missed November’s matches for the Springboks.

“Tadhg got off free for the same thing Jan-Hendrik did. I don’t want to go into details because I’m not a legal person, but from a South African point of view, that hurt,” added Erasmus.

“I’m telling you now for any neutral – and I’m not saying the neutrals are right – but for anybody that looks at that situation on exactly the same two things that happened, one guy’s word was taken, and another guy’s word was not taken.”

“One guy got nine weeks. He didn’t play for the Springboks, and the other guy played the next weekend. That’s all I’m saying.”

On the weekend Erasmus switched his starting front row for his reserve front row at the last minute (again, after the same nonsence in Cape Town against NZ), leading to the becoming-normal sight of three starters wearing reserve jersey numbers. RugbyPass reports on the team naming shenanigans.

The coach said “I’ll say it honest” (a classic clue) before launching into an explanation for the Paris change at his latest press conference, and explained why he names his teams earlier in the week than other Test sides.

The explanation wasn’t prompted by a question about his tactics, but by one on another famous habit of his: naming his opponents’ matchday 23 before they do.

“I get into trouble when I do that. People say I’m arrogant,” he grinned. “I’ve got a fairly good idea.”

“That’s why we announce our team on Monday, and I get into trouble when we change things. We announce it on a Monday, and I’ll say it honest, for us as a team environment, if a team isn’t announced on a Monday, the speculation is Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and it gets into the camp. And the players have social media and see ‘I think this guy should be playing’.

“You announce it internally on a Sunday night so players don’t get pulled into that vibe of ‘but I should get a chance’. That’s how we operate a Springboks team, while one team is playing, the other is supporting.”

“Why do we change props after Thursday? Because we see the team they’ve picked, and Julien Marchand would have played, and when we saw this we thought let’s make a change. We probably could have done that when they announce the team on Thursday, but the laws say you can do it the next morning before the game.”

“This is honest, we thought, okay, let’s get Jan-Hendrik (Wessels), Thomas (du Toit) and Gerhard (Steenekamp) at the stadium; maybe we need them next year at the World Cup under pressure starting a big Test match for us, and they’re going to play against one of the best scrummaging hookers, and then he went through just before the game.“

“And that’s why we changed them; we announced our team, they brought out a team on Thursday, we thought okay, this is going to be proper pressure for Jan-Hendrik.”

“If people are going to keep getting upset about that, I’m apologising – I’m not apologising that I’m doing it, I’m apologising that you’re going to get upset, always.“

Boffins discover blood markers for advanced CTE

Brain damage evidence isn’t just a Friday thing on the GAGR website. The Guardian reports that Scientists are a step closer to diagnosing the degenerative brain condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in living people, after a study found a blood biomarker that identifies an advanced form of the disease.

Scientists at Washington University School of Medicine in St Louis have now identified a protein fragment in blood – eMTBR-tau243 – that is elevated not only in Alzheimer’s disease but also in other brain diseases that share the same type of toxic protein buildup, including CTE.

“We are potentially opening a new door for diagnosing and treating CTE in living patients,” said Kanta Horie, the co-senior author of the study in the medical journal JAMA Neurology.

When researchers tested blood from 11 people whose CTE was confirmed at autopsy, they found that levels of eMTBR-tau243 were higher than in healthy people and rose with the severity of the brain disease.

The test could distinguish people with advanced CTE from healthy people with high accuracy, but it could not reliably identify early-stage CTE.

The scientists say that if large studies confirm their findings, clinicians could use such a blood test to monitor people at risk from CTE and enable trials of drugs that could help the condition.

“Our study shows that an Alzheimer’s disease biomarker can be applied to other tauopathies, including CTE,” the neuroscientist Chihiro Sato, who co-authored the study with Horie, said. “This is not going to be a standalone biomarker. But if someone has a history of repeated head injury, tests negative for Alzheimer’s and this biomarker comes up, it might be CTE.”
